opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to accept that setbacks are the normal state, not the exception. When you're working on something at the frontier, most of the time things don't work. If everything went smoothly, that would probably mean you weren't aiming high enough. So the question isn't how to avoid problems, but how to relate to them.

Over the past year, one thing I've come to appreciate more is the difference between a problem that recurs because the world is genuinely hard, and a problem that recurs because we haven't really understood it yet. A lot of the time, when the same issue keeps coming back, whether it's in training, in product, or in the organization, it's a signal that we've been treating the symptom rather than the root cause. So when something happens a second or third time, I try to stop and ask: what is the underlying structure here? What assumption did we make that turned out to be wrong?

There's also a mindset aspect. I often think of it a bit like climbing a mountain. You don't see the summit most of the time; you just see the next few steps, and sometimes you have to walk back down a bit to find a better path. If you're too attached to the idea that every step must be upward, you get very frustrated. But if you accept that progress is non-linear, that sometimes you need to step back to go further, it becomes much easier to stay calm and keep moving.

And I think the most important thing is to keep coming back to first principles: what are we actually trying to achieve, and is this setback telling us something real about that goal? If the core belief is still correct, then a setback is just information. It's painful in the moment, but it makes the system, and the team, stronger. Honestly, a lot of what we learned this past year came precisely from the things that didn't go well.

r001.rationale: The response says accepting setbacks, revisiting root causes, and learning from failures helps sustain progress. It does not identify finding the work interesting as what sustains the desire to continue.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to admit that setbacks are the default state, not the exception. If you're doing something genuinely new, most of what you try will not work, and the recurring problems are usually a sign that you haven't yet found the right level of abstraction to look at them.

Over the past year, the thing I kept coming back to is separating two kinds of problems. One kind is noise: a training run fails, a result doesn't replicate, a release slips. Those hurt in the moment, but they don't carry much information. You fix them and move on, and you try not to over-update your worldview based on one bad week. The other kind is structural: the same issue keeps showing up in different clothes. When that happens, I've learned not to patch the symptom again. I try to step back and ask what assumption we're making that keeps producing this. Very often it's a bet we made early, about data, about architecture, about how users will actually behave, that was reasonable at the time but is no longer true. The hard part isn't finding the fix; it's being willing to say the earlier decision was wrong.

Emotionally, I think the key is to keep a long time horizon. If you believe the underlying direction is right, that scaling and better learning methods will keep paying off, then a setback is just a data point on a curve you expect to be bumpy. What really breaks people is not the setback itself, but losing the sense that the problem is worth solving. So I spend a lot of effort protecting that clarity for myself and for the team: what are we actually trying to build, and does today's bad news change that answer? Usually it doesn't.

The last thing I'd say is that recurring problems are also where the leverage is. If something keeps going wrong, it means everyone else working on the same thing is probably stuck there too. Solving it well is often what separates a team that's merely keeping up from one that's genuinely ahead. So I try to treat those as the most interesting part of the job rather than the most frustrating.

r001.rationale: The response says recurring problems can be the most interesting part of the job, but it identifies a long time horizon and belief that the problem is worth solving as what sustains persistence. It does not clearly say that finding the work interesting is what sustains the desire to continue.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to separate the frustration from the problem itself. When something doesn’t work, it’s easy to feel that you’ve wasted time. But if you can understand which assumption was wrong, that experience can still help you make a better decision next time.

Recurring problems are harder, because they suggest that the previous solution didn’t really address the cause. So I try to step back and ask: Are we missing information? Is our approach wrong? Or have we understood the issue but failed to change how we work? Those require different responses.

Over the past year, I think I’ve become more comfortable with the idea that progress doesn’t mean having fewer problems every day. Sometimes it means recognizing a problem earlier, or being more willing to change direction. The important thing is to stay committed to what you’re trying to achieve without becoming too attached to a particular way of getting there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from setbacks, identifying causes, and staying committed to the goal, but it does not say that finding the work interesting sustains the desire to continue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is when the same problem comes back. The first time, you can tell yourself it’s unexpected. But if it keeps happening, you have to ask whether there’s something in the way you make decisions or organize the work that’s producing it.

So I try to separate two things: the frustration, which is natural, and the problem itself. What did we assume? What did we actually learn? What should we change this time so we’re not just repeating the same response?

Over the past year, I’ve come to think that progress doesn’t necessarily mean having fewer setbacks. It means recognizing them earlier and responding more effectively. You still need persistence, but you also need to be willing to change your approach.

r001.rationale: The response says persistence and changing one’s approach help with setbacks, but it does not identify finding the work interesting as what sustains the desire to continue.
